::: {.lead}
A film tells every viewer the same story. A game can do more. In some games,
every player follows the same road. In others, the player's choices change
what happens and how the story ends. And in many games, nobody tells the
story at all: the player finds it in the rooms, the objects and the places
of the game world. In lectures 3 and 4 you learned the building blocks of a
story and placed them on the stages of a game. In this lesson you meet the
three main ways in which games tell a story: **linear**, **branching** and
**environmental** storytelling, and the effect of each one on the player.
Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary linear-narrative branching-narrative branch-and-bottleneck player-agency environmental-storytelling narrative-structure story-beat player-experience >}}

## 5.1 One road through the story: linear narrative

In *Moon Diver* (lecture 4), every player meets the same eight stages in the
same order: the alarm, the map, the caves … the guardian, the lights. The
player decides *how* to dive through each stage, but not *what* happens in
the story. This is a **linear narrative** (@fig-linear).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.1 — Linear narrative"}
A **linear narrative** is a story that every player meets in the same order,
with the same events and the same ending.
:::

![A linear narrative: one road through the story.](images/linear.png){#fig-linear width=94%}

A linear story has clear strengths. The writer controls the order of the
beats, so the tension curve of lecture 4 works exactly as planned. The
climax comes at the right moment. And the team writes each scene only once,
so it costs less. Most mobile games with a story are linear. The weakness:
the player cannot change the story. Some players want their decisions to
matter.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.1 — Is Moon Diver linear?"}
1. Every player sees the eight stages in the same order.
2. The player chooses the path through the ice caves and the moment to
   escape from the eels: these are gameplay choices.
3. No choice changes the story or the ending. So the narrative is linear,
   but the gameplay is still free.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Linear means boring." A linear story with a good hook, rests and a late
climax can be very exciting. Linear describes the *structure* of the story,
not its quality.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Linear or not?"}
Choose a game with a story that you have played.

1. Write two choices that you made while playing.
2. For each choice, write: did it change the story (what happens), or only
   the gameplay (how you play)?

*Your result:* the game, two choices, and one sentence: is its narrative
linear?
:::

## 5.2 Choices that change the story: branching narrative

In a **branching narrative**, the player's choices lead to different scenes.
Different players can see different events and different endings. When
choices really change the story, the player feels **agency**: "what I do
matters".

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.2 — Branching narrative"}
A **branching narrative** is a story in which the player's choices lead to
different scenes and endings.
:::

Branching has a cost. Each new choice opens new scenes, and the writers must
make all of them. With two options at each decision, the scenes double at
every step (@fig-branch, left). Writers therefore often let the paths
**join again** at key scenes. This is called **branch and bottleneck**
(@fig-branch, right). The player still makes real choices, but the writers
make far fewer scenes.

![A full tree and a branch-and-bottleneck structure, both with three choices of two options.](images/branching.png){#fig-branch width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.2 — How many scenes?"}
A story has 3 decisions in a row, each with 2 options.

1. Full tree: 1 start, then 2, 4 and 8 scenes: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15$ scenes,
   and 8 endings. One player sees only 4 of them.
2. Branch and bottleneck: 1 start, 2 options, 1 joining scene, 2 options,
   1 joining scene, 2 endings: 9 scenes and 2 endings.
3. The writers save 6 scenes. Each player still makes 3 choices.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.3 — The map of Silent Station"}
In the made-up game *Silent Station* (case study), Mira first chooses:
follow the footprints, or repair the radio. Both paths end at the antenna on
the hill: the bottleneck. There she chooses again, and the story has two
endings.

1. Scenes: arrival, 2 first-choice scenes, the antenna, 2 endings: 6 scenes.
2. Endings: 2. Choices for each player: 2.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Fake choices. If both options lead to the same scene *and* nothing is
different there, the player feels tricked. At a bottleneck, the earlier
choice should still leave a mark: a line of dialogue, an object, a
character who remembers.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/branch-builder.html" poster="sims/branch-builder.png" title="Branch Builder: how many scenes must the writers make?" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Branch Builder"}
Open the **Branch Builder** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Set 2 choices and 3 decisions. Write the scenes and the endings for a
   full tree, then for branch and bottleneck.
2. Change to 3 choices and do it again.

*Your result:* four rows of numbers, and one sentence: why do writers let
paths join?
:::

## 5.3 The world tells the story: environmental storytelling

Mira arrives at an empty station in the desert. Nobody talks to her, and no
film plays. But the room tells her what happened (@fig-room): a full cup of
cold tea, a burnt radio, a day circled on the calendar, footprints in the
sand. This is **environmental storytelling**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.3 — Environmental storytelling"}
**Environmental storytelling** tells a story through the places and objects
of the game world. The player discovers it by exploring.
:::

![The empty room of Silent Station. Five objects tell what happened.](images/station-room.png){#fig-room width=94%}

Environmental storytelling has three strengths for the player experience.
The player finds the story actively, like a detective. It does not stop the
gameplay, as a long cutscene does. And it works together with a linear or a
branching story. Its tools are objects, notes, damage, light, sound, and
the place where things are.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.4 — Reading the room"}
1. A full cup of cold tea: someone left in a hurry.
2. A burnt radio: nobody could call for help.
3. "Supply truck" circled yesterday: the truck did not come.
4. A note, "Gone to fix the antenna. Back by 6. – Aziz", and footprints to
   the door: Aziz went to the hill and did not come back.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Objects that tell nothing. A plant or a chair in the room is just
decoration. A clue must fit the story and point to an event. Too many
random objects hide the real clues.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the clues"}
Choose one place in a game that you know (or the room above).

1. List three objects or details of the place.
2. For each one, write what it tells about the story.

*Your result:* three rows: object, what it tells.
:::

## Case study: Silent Station

*Silent Station* is a made-up mobile game. Mira, a radio operator, arrives
at a small research station in the desert. Nobody is there. The room tells
what happened: a cup of cold tea, a note from Aziz ("Gone to fix the
antenna. Back by 6."), a burnt radio, a circled day ("supply truck") and
footprints to the door. Then Mira chooses: **follow the footprints** or
**repair the radio first**. Both paths lead to the antenna on the hill,
where Aziz sits with a hurt foot. There she chooses again: **help Aziz fix
the antenna** (ending A: help is coming) or **take Aziz back to the station
first** (ending B: a safe, silent night). The game mixes all three ways of
telling a story. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this
story. In the mini-game below you explore the room and play both paths.

{{< sim file="sims/silent-station.html" poster="sims/silent-station.png" title="Silent Station: explore the room, then choose" kind="game" height="780" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on story and on
indirect control (how the world guides the player); and the chapter on the
story machine (choices and branching).

## Exercises

1. What is a linear narrative? Give one strength and one weakness.
2. A player chooses which weapon to use, but the story is always the same.
   Is the narrative linear or branching? Why?
3. What is player agency?
4. A story has 2 decisions in a row, each with 2 options, as a full tree.
   How many endings does it have? How many scenes?
5. Why do writers use branch and bottleneck?
6. What is a fake choice? How can a writer avoid it at a bottleneck?
7. What is environmental storytelling? Name three of its tools.
8. In a game, a hallway has a broken door, a long scratch on the wall and an
   empty cage. What story can these objects tell?
9. *Silent Station*: which part is environmental storytelling, and where is
   the bottleneck?
10. How many endings does *Silent Station* have, and how many scenes?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A story that every player meets in the same order with the same ending. Strength: the writer controls the tension and it costs less. Weakness: the player cannot change the story.
2. Linear: the choice changes only the gameplay, not the story.
3. The player's feeling that their choices really change what happens.
4. 4 endings; 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 scenes.
5. The paths join again at key scenes, so the writers need far fewer scenes, but the player still makes real choices.
6. A choice that changes nothing. The earlier choice should leave a mark at the bottleneck (a line of dialogue, an object, a character who remembers).
7. Telling the story through places and objects that the player discovers. Tools: objects, notes, damage, light, sound, the place of things.
8. For example: an animal broke out of its cage, scratched the wall and broke the door.
9. The room (cup, note, radio, calendar, footprints). The bottleneck is the antenna on the hill.
10. 2 endings; 6 scenes (arrival, 2 first-choice scenes, the antenna, 2 endings).
:::
